lesson_title: Sorting the Washing: Collecting and Summarising Data
hook_text: The average wait was 36 minutes. The typical wait was 30. Both are true — and only one of them is honest.
clip_script: A taxi rank. Fifteen commuters. Somebody timed how long each one queued, and the list came back jumbled — useless. So do what you do with washing: sort it first. Six, twelve, fifteen, eighteen... all the way up to ninety-six. Now the story shows itself — a crowd of short-to-middling waits, and three that ran away completely. Share all the minutes out equally and you get an average of 36 minutes. But line everyone up shortest to longest and the person standing dead in the middle waited only 30. Why the gap? Because three commuters stood for 60, 72 and 96 minutes, and those long waits haul the average up — the same way one cousin with a big contract phone hauls up the family's average airtime spend while everyone else buys R30 vouchers. The middle number doesn't get hauled. So when somebody quotes you an average, ask what the middle is. If they're far apart, somebody at the edges is doing the pulling — and that's usually the real story.
visual_style: A taxi rank at dawn, then fifteen numbered cards shuffling themselves into a neat ascending line; three cards at the far end glowing red as an average marker slides toward them while a median marker stays put.
mood: Curious and quietly revealing — the satisfaction of seeing a hidden story surface.
pacing: Unhurried sorting rhythm, a beat of stillness at the two numbers, sharp punch on the closing warning.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and learn which average is telling you the truth.
